channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
gist: Jason Calacanis and Lon Harris run a fantasy-draft style game picking five companies Apple should buy under new CEO John Turnis (ElevenLabs, Disney, Sony, Perplexity, Boston Dynamics, DigitalOcean, Etched, Lucid, Superhuman, Go AI and more), with audience picks, followed by an interview with the founder of UV-tracking wearable the 90.

insights.claim: Apple historically makes small tuck-in acquisitions of technical teams (such as the teams behind Siri and Touch ID) and prioritizes buying back its own stock, rather than acquiring robust full products.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline that a large acquisition would be a regime change for Apple capital allocation.

insights.claim: Jason argues Apple's new CEO John Turnis should stop buying back shares and take massively big swings, targeting anything the iPhone, laptop, watch, AirPods and Apple stores can integrate with.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A capital-allocation pivot from buybacks to large deals would change the Apple equity story and could hit acquisition targets' valuations.
insights.quote: I believe John Turner should stop buying back the shares and should take massively big swings.

insights.claim: Apple is described as having about $250 billion in cash and a roughly $4.96 trillion market cap, so every named target (all in the $5-150 billion range) is smaller than its cash position, and a $50 billion deal is about 1% of market cap.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Affordability is not the constraint on Apple megadeals; regulators and integration are.

insights.claim: Jason wants acquisitions that could build a $100 billion to $500 billion revenue stream to reduce iPhone dependency, and dismisses small tuck-ins like Sonos, Spotify or Whoop as not changing the company's fortunes.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames iPhone concentration as the strategic problem that acquisitions are supposed to solve.
insights.quote: I'm looking for things that could build a hundred billion, a $200 billion, a $500 billion revenue stream.

themes.theme: AI voice, model routing and local inference

insights.claim: Lon picks ElevenLabs (last valued roughly $5-10 billion) as Apple's top target: with voice mode coming and Siri needing a fix, a voice-commanded phone (for example while driving) is table stakes for Apple.
insights.speaker: co-host Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Voice is framed as the next primary interface, and ElevenLabs is seen as the clear voice-quality leader.

insights.claim: Jason argues Perplexity is a natural Apple buy because Apple is not tied to one model family and can be model agnostic, using Perplexity as the router for any model, plus its agents, its own search engine and a possible replacement for the Google default-search deal when it runs out.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Implies that Apple's Google search default arrangement and its model neutrality make an AI-search acquisition plausible.
insights.quote: they can afford to be totally model agnostic and Perplexity would be the perfect router

insights.claim: Lon picks Etched (valued around $21 billion) as an inference chip company: Apple depends on Nvidia like everyone else and its server-side AI runs on Apple Silicon not designed for inference at billions of devices, so an AI chip acquisition would add Nvidia-level talent without buying an Nvidia-sized company.
insights.speaker: co-host Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Signals inference-specific silicon as a strategic asset and Etched as a possible takeout candidate.

insights.claim: Jason picks his portfolio company Go AI (local AI) as his fifth pick, arguing local, on-device AI is the big winner; ExoLabs was named as an alternative that could also fit.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: On-device AI is a recurring theme across host and audience picks (Liquid AI, Prism ML too), suggesting perceived value in local inference for Apple's privacy positioning. Note Go AI is a disclosed portfolio company of the host.

insights.claim: Audience contributors also favored AI infrastructure targets for Apple: Perplexity, World Labs (spatial intelligence) and Prism ML (shrinking large models to run locally) from one; ElevenLabs from another; Liquid AI (on-device models for latency, power or no-network constraints) and Kagi (privacy-first paid search) from another.
insights.speaker: audience contributors
insights.so_what: Shows which private AI companies the startup community views as strategic for Apple; convergence on Perplexity and ElevenLabs.

insights.claim: One audience contributor argued Apple acquires when a technology becomes important enough to experience, citing NeXT (OS foundation of Mac OS and iOS), PA Semi (silicon capability that let it move off Intel) and PrimeSense (3D sensing behind Face ID), and expects agents to create the same kind of moment.
insights.speaker: audience contributor David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Provides a pattern for predicting Apple acquisitions: platform-level capability shifts, not products.

insights.claim: Jason picks Disney (about $182 billion market cap) to integrate all Disney content into an Apple One bundle, theme park interactivity via the phone, Disney-branded Apple hardware, and IP in the stores, citing Apple TV's recent progress with shows.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Speculative content-plus-hardware bundle idea; a Disney deal would be the largest media acquisition candidate discussed.

insights.claim: Lon picks Sony (about $135 billion market cap) for PlayStation (an installed base in millions of homes), Sony Pictures, Sony Music and Crunchyroll, the leading anime streaming service in the West, which he says would let Apple be the distributor of nearly every popular anime series and become a Netflix rival.
insights.speaker: co-host Lon Harris
insights.so_what: A gaming, music and anime bundle would give Apple a large content and distribution footprint.

insights.claim: Jason picks Boston Dynamics (which he says has an interim CEO) on the view that Apple will eventually have to have a robot and that people would trust an Apple robot in their home; if it sold 100 million robots a year it could be transformative.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Humanoid or home robots are seen as a new hardware category where brand trust is the differentiator.
insights.quote: eventually Apple will have no choice but to have a robot

insights.claim: Jason picks DigitalOcean (valued around $10-20 billion, implying about a $25 billion deal with a 50% premium) to give Apple a cloud hosting arm for developers using MacBooks, competing with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and says it could become a $50-100 billion revenue line.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Speculates on Apple entering cloud infrastructure; the revenue estimates are the host's own guesses, not analysis.

insights.claim: Jason chooses EV maker Lucid (over Rivian) for Apple, noting Lucid is reportedly working on a dedicated robotaxi (cyber cab); he says Waymo, BMW, Mercedes and Cursor are not available, and Tesla is too big.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Illustrates the transportation angle, with autonomy and robotaxi capability as the reason to own a car maker.

insights.claim: Lon picks Superhuman (the Grammarly-owned email and productivity app) so Apple could upgrade its mail, writing and productivity apps overnight, with Superhuman Go as a MacBook mail client.
insights.speaker: co-host Lon Harris
insights.so_what: AI-native productivity apps are seen as an upgrade path for Apple's stale first-party apps.

insights.claim: Jason rules out health and wearables targets Peloton, Whoop and Aura because the Apple Watch already covers the sensors and it would create tension, and treats Formula 1 and Nintendo as wild cards; Lon says leagues like the NFL or NBA cannot be bought since they are franchise groups.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Shows what the hosts consider overlapping with Apple's existing products, and thus poor acquisition fits.

themes.theme: The 90 UV wearable and sunlight data

insights.claim: The 90 sells a $299 modular pendant that measures UVA and UVB with separate sensors and, through an app, gives a live UV reading, vitamin D and circadian light tracking, and a sun score with burn, aging and 'sun debt' metrics; the price includes the app with no subscription, and the host suggests trying a $10 per month subscription option.
insights.speaker: guest Stacy Salvi, co-founder and CEO of the 90
insights.so_what: Consumer health wearables are moving to single-signal specialty sensors; the business model debate (hardware plus optional subscription) is live.

insights.claim: The founder says UV exposure causes about 90% of photoaging, that about 60 health conditions (including eczema, psoriasis, lupus and vitiligo) are impacted by sunlight, and that skin keeps processing a heavy sun day for up to 5 days.
insights.speaker: guest Stacy Salvi, co-founder and CEO of the 90
insights.so_what: These are the founder's claims and are unverified here; they define the addressable health-data thesis.
insights.quote: There are about 60 different health conditions that are impacted by sunlight.

insights.claim: Jason argues on-body UV data at scale (1,000 to 100,000 wearers with ethnicity, location, heart rate and weight) would be valuable to pharma and university researchers, and the founder says inbound research interest exists and her chief medical officer is Dr. Richard Weller of the University of Edinburgh, who found lower COVID mortality in areas with higher UV index.
insights.speaker: host Jason Calacanis and guest Stacy Salvi
insights.so_what: The data-licensing angle could matter more than hardware sales if a large enough cohort is built.

insights.claim: Stacy Salvi previously spent about eight years at Fitbit (through the Google acquisition) and then worked at a publicly traded smart ring startup, Mavano, which won 16 best of CES awards; Jason notes Fitbit has been renamed Google Health and that he nearly lost his 20-year weight history in the transition.
insights.speaker: guest Stacy Salvi, co-founder and CEO of the 90
insights.so_what: Founder background in wearables, plus a data-portability risk when platforms rebrand or migrate.

insights.claim: Stacy says there is currently a lot of distrust of sunscreens driven by recent large research studies, and the 90 positions itself to measure and inform rather than recommend specific sunscreens.
insights.speaker: guest Stacy Salvi, co-founder and CEO of the 90
insights.so_what: Consumer skepticism of sunscreen chemistry is a tailwind for measurement and alternative sun-protection products.
